PHSCS 587

Inversion-layer quantization

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a surface confinement potential gives carriers discrete energy subbands

Carriers confined near the oxide interface do not have arbitrary energy for motion normal to the surface. A quantum calculation gives subband energies and wavefunctions, changing both population and the depth at which inversion charge sits.

In the nMOS model discussed here, raising the lowest allowed carrier energies reduces inversion charge at a given classical surface potential. Additional surface potential Δψs is needed to reach the selected inversion condition. A local gate conversion gives ΔVth ≈ mΔψs.

This correction is distinct from depletion inside a polysilicon gate. A narrow-body device may also have confinement from its finite silicon thickness. The often-used 1/t² energy scaling belongs to an ideal infinite well; actual oxide barriers, effective masses and electrostatics require a self-consistent model.

Example

If a particular quantum calculation gives an additional surface potential of 50 mV and the local body factor is m = 1.2, the corresponding gate threshold correction is approximately +60 mV.

Sources and scope
  • PHSCS 587 reading: 5.3–5.4, quantum effect on threshold

Practice

1. Why does a subband energy shift affect charge density even when the classical electric field is unchanged?

Carrier occupancy depends on allowed energy states relative to the chemical potential.

Changing the allowed energies changes the occupation of those states. The same classical potential therefore need not produce the same inversion population.
